To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
cholinergic neuronal loss is a major component of Alzheimer’s disease and is also a component of Parkinson’s disease.

in vivo cholinergic terminal density is reduced in the cerebral cortex of patients with Alzheimer's Disease and Parkinson's Disease, but not in patients with Parkinson's Disease who do not have dementia.

in vivo mapping of choline acetyitransferase activity in normal aging and Alzheimer's disease has revealed that cholinergic neurons are not as devastated as suggested by post mortem studies of choline acethyltransferase activity, and that the pattern of cholinergic deficit in Parkinson's disease differs according to the age at onset of dementia.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development and evaluation of new methods for the diagnosis of Alzheimer's disease ( AD ).

the role of cholinergic systems in the regulation of memory, learning and attention, and with the role of these systems in the pathophysiology of Alzheimer’s Disease (AD) and Parkinson’s Disease (PD).
the study of brain aging, and the role of cholinergic dysfunction in dementia.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the IBVM SPECT technique is a valuable tool for in vivo assessment of cholinergic neuron function and integrity in normal aging, AD, and PD.
the cholinergic deficit in Alzheimer’s disease is not a consequence of normal aging.

the IBVM SPECT technique is a valuable method to study cholinergic terminal integrity in vivo, but that the results should be interpreted with caution and in conjunction with other methods, eg, ChAT, PET, or MRI, to avoid misinterpretation.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

cholinergic terminal integrity can be assessed in living human subjects, and that in AD, the integrity of cholinergic projections to cerebral cortex and hippocampal formation is not so devastated as suggested by ChAT activity (50-70% decline).

the cholinergic deficit in AD and PD is not as devastating as postmortem ChAT activity measurements would indicate, that the loss of cholinergic innervation in AD is not uniform, and that cholinergic deficits in AD and PD are not the same.

the loss of cholinergic nerve terminals in AD and PD is not as severe as suggested by post-mortem ChAT activity, and that in vivo mapping of choline transporter density can reveal the extent and topography of cholinergic deficit in these disorders.
The main takeaway from our work is that

we have developed a method that allows us to map the cholinergic system non-invasively, and we have used this method to show that the cholinergic systems in Alzheimer’s and Parkinson’s disease patients are not as devastated as we thought.
we have a new tool that can be used to assess cholinergic function in living patients.
cholinergic deficits in AD are not uniform, but are more pronounced in the temporal lobe and hippocampus in early-onset disease, and more widespread in late-onset disease.
